opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important concern, and one I take seriously. The tasks in our suite are mostly well-specified software engineering, machine learning engineering, and cybersecurity tasks. They have relatively clean success criteria, because that's what lets us score them reliably and compare across models and against human baselines. But a lot of what might bottleneck recursive self-improvement isn't like that.

If you think about what actually drives AI research progress, a big part of it is the messier stuff: choosing which research directions to pursue, having good taste about which experiments are worth running, interpreting noisy results, noticing when something surprising is going on, and coordinating work over weeks or months without a clear signal of whether you're on the right track. Our benchmark has some tasks that gesture at this, but by construction it's biased toward things you can automatically check. So there's a real possibility that models get very good at the tasks we measure while still being weak at the parts that matter most for speeding up AI R&D. Or, in the other direction, that capabilities in those messier areas improve in ways our metrics don't pick up.

There are a few things I'd say in response. First, we've tried to be upfront that the time-horizon measure is one piece of evidence, not a complete picture. It tells you something about how long and how complex the tasks models can complete autonomously are, in a particular distribution. Extrapolating from that to "can this model meaningfully accelerate AI research" takes extra assumptions, and people should be careful about that.

Second, there's some reason to think the capabilities are correlated. Being able to stay coherent over long tasks, recover from errors, and manage complex codebases seems like a prerequisite for a lot of research work. So progress on our tasks probably isn't irrelevant to recursive self-improvement, even if it isn't sufficient.

Third, the obvious answer is that we need complementary measurements. That includes tasks that are more open-ended and closer to real research, studies of how much models actually speed up researchers in practice, and qualitative evaluation where people look closely at what the model is doing rather than just a pass/fail score. Each has its own problems: they're expensive, noisier, and harder to compare over time. But if the question is whether we're approaching something like automated AI R&D, I don't think any single clean benchmark will settle it. You want several lines of evidence, and you want to pay particular attention to the places where they disagree.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts METR’s well-specified, automatically checkable tasks with less measurable research capabilities such as choosing directions, interpreting noisy results, and coordinating long-term work.

r002.rationale: The candidate says some measured abilities may correlate with research capabilities, but does not suggest that diversity across benchmark tasks is what makes performance predictive of unmeasured capabilities.

r003.rationale: The candidate proposes complementary evaluations but does not propose examining variation in model performance across METR’s benchmark tasks to assess generalization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's a fair concern, and honestly it's one I share to some extent. The time horizon metric we're measuring is really about autonomous task completion on software and research-engineering tasks, and we've been pretty explicit that it's a proxy. It's not a direct measurement of "can this model do the specific things that would let it meaningfully speed up its own development."

There are a few ways the benchmark could miss what matters. One is that our tasks are pretty self-contained. They have clear specifications, they're scored automatically, and the agent is working in a fresh environment with a well-defined goal. A lot of real AI R&D doesn't look like that. It's messy, it involves figuring out what question to even ask, iterating with other people, dealing with ambiguous or contradictory results over weeks. We've tried to address some of that with things like RE-Bench, where the tasks are more open-ended ML engineering problems, but those are still much more structured than real research.

Another thing is that recursive self-improvement, if it happens, is probably bottlenecked on a fairly narrow set of capabilities, and it's not obvious our task distribution samples those well. Things like research taste, knowing which experiments are worth running, noticing when something is subtly wrong with your setup. Those are hard to turn into a benchmark task with an automated grader. So there's a real possibility that models get good at exactly those things, or fail to, in a way our numbers don't track.

What I'd say in defense of the approach is that it's not meant to be the whole picture. The time horizon trend is useful because it's measurable and it's been surprisingly consistent, which gives you something to extrapolate from. But we try to pair it with other kinds of evidence: uplift studies where we look at how much faster humans actually get with model assistance, qualitative work looking at the kinds of failures models have, and talking to people at labs about what they're seeing internally. If those start to diverge from the benchmark trend, that's exactly the signal that the benchmark is missing something important.

So I'd put it this way: I think the concern is right, and the honest response is to treat the benchmark as one input and keep investing in measuring the harder-to-measure stuff, rather than to pretend the number captures everything.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes METR’s measured autonomous task completion from harder-to-measure R&D bottlenecks, but it does not ask how those capabilities differ.

r002.rationale: It says the benchmark’s task distribution may fail to sample key bottlenecks; it does not suggest task diversity could make benchmark performance predictive of unmeasured capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not propose examining variation in model performance across benchmark tasks to assess generalization.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real concern. There’s a distinction between measuring whether models can do longer software tasks and measuring whether they can do the particular research that would let them improve the next generation of models. Those seem related, but I wouldn’t assume they’re interchangeable.

You could imagine a model doing very well on the benchmark while still being bad at choosing promising research directions or interpreting ambiguous experimental results. And you could also imagine a model being unusually good at some narrow part of AI research that turns out to be very useful for accelerating progress, without that showing up particularly clearly in its overall benchmark score.

So I’d want to see more direct evaluations of AI research ability, alongside the broader task evaluations. Can the model come up with an improvement, test it, and establish that it actually works? How much human guidance does that require? And then there’s a further question about whether those improvements make the system better at producing subsequent improvements. That feedback loop is what you ultimately care about for recursive self-improvement.

I think the benchmark can provide useful evidence. I’d just be cautious about treating it as a sufficient measure of how close we are to that feedback loop.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes METR’s longer software task evaluations from capabilities for AI research that could improve future models.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark performance may provide useful evidence, but does not suggest that task diversity could make it predictive of unmeasured capabilities.

r003.rationale: It proposes direct evaluations of AI research ability, but does not propose examining variation across METR benchmark tasks to assess generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real concern. I’d distinguish between measuring whether models can complete increasingly long tasks and measuring whether they can do the particular things that would let them accelerate AI research. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

You could imagine a model that’s very good at implementing an experiment when you tell it exactly what to do, but much worse at deciding which experiment is worth running or recognizing that a result undermines its approach. If one of those abilities is the bottleneck, then improvements on a broader task benchmark might not translate into much acceleration. And the reverse is possible: a model could become much more useful for AI research without that showing up proportionately on the benchmark.

So I’d treat METR’s results as evidence about a relevant capability trend, rather than a direct measurement of how close we are to recursive self-improvement. To assess that, I’d want evaluations closer to the actual research process, including whether models can choose promising directions, run experiments, interpret the results, and produce improvements that hold up under independent testing.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes completing increasingly long tasks from choosing, interpreting, and improving AI research, explaining how the benchmark may miss bottleneck capabilities.

r002.rationale: It calls METR results evidence about a relevant trend, but does not suggest that task diversity could make its benchmark predictive of unmeasured capabilities.

r003.rationale: It proposes evaluations of the research process, but does not propose examining performance variation across METR benchmark tasks.
